spec.head: Applying DeepSeek-R1 requires robust reward signals, significant comp…
body: Applying the DeepSeek-R1 recipe depends on whether your project performs pure reinforcement learning on a base model or distills existing reasoning data into a smaller checkpoint.
Direct RL demands deterministic verification and sufficient model capacity. Small models enter repetitive loops unless trained via supervised distillation.
spec.hint: Select a row to see the requirements and practical trade-offs.

rows.label: Base model scale
rows.note: Pure RL failed on 7B dense and 16B MoE models, yielding repetitive token loops. Successful RL required 32B dense or massive MoE checkpoints like 671B DeepSeek-V3. Smaller models only succeeded through SFT distillation.

rows.label: Reward feedback
rows.note: Direct RL requires unambiguous verifiers such as math solvers or compilers. Neural reward models suffer from reward hacking when scaled beyond a few hundred steps.

rows.label: Training data needs
rows.note: The full pipeline combines cold-start reasoning traces, RL prompt sets, and 800,000 curated SFT trajectories. Distillation simply fine-tunes base models directly on those exported teacher trajectories.

rows.label: Compute requirements
rows.note: RL on large models generated thousands of long rollouts up to 32,768 tokens across hundreds of steps. Distillation runs standard supervised fine-tuning over 800k examples for 2-3 epochs.

rows.label: Prompting style
rows.note: The paper notes that few-shot prompting consistently hurts reasoning performance across both settings. Users should supply zero-shot instructions and specify desired output formats directly.

args.summary: Applying DeepSeek-R1 requires large base models, robust programmatic reward signals, and significant compute resources.

args.brief: Comparison of reinforcement learning application between language model reasoning and robotic control, highlighting differences in action spaces and environment feedback.

spec.head: The paper does not test robotics, but the RL principles may apply.
body: DeepSeek-R1 relies on rule-based outcome verifiers over discrete text tokens, where sampling is cheap and fast.
Applying pure reinforcement learning to physical robotics faces distinct constraints in simulation fidelity, safety, and action space.
spec.hint: Select a row to see key operational differences.

rows.label: Action space
rows.note: Language models sample discrete tokens from a finite vocabulary, whereas physical robot policies typically operate in continuous multi-joint action spaces.

rows.label: Environment
rows.note: LLM generation updates a symbolic prompt buffer deterministically. Robotics interacts with continuous, noisy physics or imperfect simulators subject to sim-to-real gaps.

rows.label: Reward verifier
rows.note: DeepSeek-R1 succeeds by evaluating rule-based ground-truth correctness at the end of a trajectory. In robotics, reward verification requires state tracking or sensor instrumentation, making reward specification harder.

rows.label: Sample collection
rows.note: Generating thousands of LLM candidate reasoning traces runs rapidly in parallel on GPU clusters. In physical robotics, sampling is limited by real-time hardware speed and wear.

rows.label: Exploration safety
rows.note: Pure trial-and-error exploration carries zero physical safety risk in text generation. In contrast, unconstrained exploration on physical robots can cause hardware collisions or damage.

args.summary: The paper does not test robotics, but the RL principles may apply.
